content.title: About
content.content: Yellow string beans are edible pods of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris) that have a bright yellow color and are prepared by boiling. They have a mild, slightly sweet flavor and a tender texture, making them popular in side dishes, salads, and soups.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Yellow beans differ from green beans only in pod color, but share a similar nutritional profile.
They are traditionally cultivated in warm regions of North and South America as well as Europe.
Ancient varieties were used by Indigenous peoples long before European colonization.
When cooked, the beans retain most of their B‑vitamins and minerals.
Yellow beans can serve as a lower‑calorie alternative to starchy side dishes.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps maintain healthy blood sugar levels.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Yellow beans contain virtually no fat, making them suitable for low‑calorie diets.

items.title: Source of plant protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving of cooked beans provides about 7 g of protein, beneficial for vegetarians and vegans.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B1, B6, and folate aid energy metabolism and support the nervous system.

items.title: Minerals: iron and magnesium
items.content: Iron contributes to hemoglobin formation, while magnesium supports muscle and nerve function.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to beans, ranging from skin rashes to severe symptoms.

items.title: Phytic acid content
items.content: Phytic acid can reduce mineral absorption; soaking beans before cooking helps mitigate this.

items.title: Gas formation
items.content: Beans can cause bloating in sensitive people; gradual introduction to the diet lessens the effect.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked yellow string beans can be tossed into salads, soups, stews, used as a side dish for meat or fish, or incorporated into vegetable casseroles. They can also be quickly sautéed with garlic and herbs for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked beans in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze them in portioned bags for up to 3 months. Discard any beans that develop an off‑smell or mold.
